claim: Rats were trained to perform a perceptual decision-making task where they listened to two simultaneous series of randomly timed auditory clicks from speakers on the left and right.
source: Rats listened to two simultaneous series of randomly timed auditory clicks, one from a speaker on the left and one from a speaker on the right.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental task design used in the study.

claim: After the end of the click train, rats had to orient to the side with a greater number of clicks to receive a reward.
source: After the end of the click train, the rat had to orient to the side with a greater number of clicks to receive a reward (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task requirement and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The study analyzed behavioral choice data and electrophysiological neural recordings from 11 rats.
source: We analyzed behavioral choice data and electrophysiological neural recordings from 11 rats.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset analyzed in the study.

claim: The study analyzed 37,179 behavioral choices and 141 neurons from three brain areas—the PPC, the FOF, and the ADS.
source: In total, we analyzed 37,179 behavioral choices and 141 neurons from three brain areas—the PPC, the FOF, and the ADS.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the total amount of data analyzed.

claim: Prior electrophysiological and lesion studies have shown that the PPC, FOF, and ADS play a key role in evidence accumulation.
source: Prior electrophysiological and lesions studies have shown that these brain regions play a key role in evidence accumulation (Ding and Gold, 2013; Ding and Gold, 2010; Erlich et al., 2015; Erlich et al., 2011; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Gold and Shadlen, 2000; Hanks et al., 2015; Huk and Shadlen, 2005; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Mante et al., 2013; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Yartsev et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Data were collected after the animals were well trained and exhibiting a high level of performance.
source: Data were collected after the animals were well trained and exhibiting a high level of performance (Brunton et al., 2013; Hanks et al., 2015; Yartsev et al., 2018); these data were collected as part of two earlier studies and have been previously analyzed (Hanks et al., 2015; Yartsev et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the training state of animals and cites prior studies that collected the data.

claim: Neurons were selected for inclusion based on significant tuning for choice during the stimulus period (two-sample t-test, p<0.01).
source: We selected neurons with significant tuning for choice during the stimulus period (two-sample t-test, p<0.01) because choice tuning is a prerequisite for reflecting accumulation-like signals.
evidence: This describes the statistical criterion used for neuron selection.

claim: The FOF dataset consisted of 68 neurons with 7382 behavioral choices recorded from five rats over 46 behavioral sessions.
source: Once tuning significance was determined, our dataset consisted of 68 neurons from FOF, with 7382 behavioral choices recorded from five rats over 46 behavioral sessions
evidence: This is a direct statement about the FOF dataset composition.

claim: The PPC dataset consisted of 25 neurons with 9037 behavioral choices from three rats over 24 sessions.
source: 25 neurons from PPC, with 9037 behavioral choices from three rats over 24 sessions
evidence: This is a direct statement about the PPC dataset composition.

claim: The ADS dataset consisted of 48 neurons with 10,760 behavioral choices from three rats over 27 behavioral sessions.
source: 48 neurons from ADS, with 10,760 behavioral choices from three rats over 27 behavioral sessions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ADS dataset composition.

claim: Positive values of λ correspond to unstable dynamics where early clicks have greater influence on a(t) than recent clicks.
source: Positive values of λ correspond to unstable dynamics so that a(t) grows exponentially. In this setting, early clicks have greater influence on a(t) than recent clicks, because their impact grows with time.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the leak parameter when positive.

claim: Negative values of λ correspond to leaky dynamics where early clicks have a weaker influence on a(t) than recent clicks.
source: By contrast, negative values of λ correspond to leaky dynamics. In this setting, early clicks have a weaker influence on a(t) than recent clicks because the impact of early clicks decays with time.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the leak parameter when negative.

claim: When λ equals zero, the sensory clicks are perfectly integrated.
source: When λ equals zero, the sensory clicks are perfectly integrated.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the leak parameter when zero.

claim: Previous results have shown that rats exhibit a range of accumulation strategies spanning different values of λ.
source: Previous results have shown that rats exhibit a range of accumulation strategies spanning these values of λ (Brunton et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The model provided an accurate account of mean responses in all three brain areas with a median R² of 0.91, 0.68, and 0.87 for the FOF, PPC, and ADS, respectively.
source: The model provided an accurate account of mean responses in all three brain areas (Figure 2B), with a median R2 of 0.91, 0.68, and 0.87 for the FOF, PPC, and ADS, respectively (Figure 2B, colored lines).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of model fit to neural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The model accurately accounted for psychophysical choice behavior with R² of 0.99 for FOF, 0.99 for PPC, and 0.97 for ADS.
source: Figure 2C shows a comparison between true psychometric curves and the psychometric curve of the fitted model, confirming that the model also accounted for psychophysical choice behavior (R2: 0.99—FOF; 0.99—PPC; ADS—0.97; see Methods for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of model fit to choice data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A shared accumulator model for each brain region is sufficient to capture the animals' choice sensitivity to the stimulus and strength of accumulated evidence reflected in each neuron's response.
source: These analyses confirm that a shared accumulator model for each brain region is sufficient to capture the animals' choice sensitivity to the stimulus and strength of accumulated evidence reflected in each neuron's response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model fitting results presented in Figure 2.

claim: Both fitted models (joint and choice-only) exhibited strong adaptation (φ<<1) consistent with prior work.
source: Both fitted models exhibited strong adaptation (ϕ<< 1) consistent with prior work fitting choice accumulator models (Brunton et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a parameter finding and cites prior work showing consistency.

claim: Strong adaptation indicates that a stimulus pulse occurring in rapid succession following other pulses has a smaller effect on a(t) than an isolated pulse.
source: This indicates that a stimulus pulse that occurs in rapid succession following other pulses has a smaller effect on a(t) than an isolated pulse.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the adaptation parameter.

claim: Large initial variance in the joint model likely reflects variability in neural responses prior to stimulus onset.
source: Large initial variance in the joint model likely reflects variability in neural responses prior to stimulus onset (Churchland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the initial variance parameter with citation to related work.

claim: Strong accumulation noise in the joint model was also found when the negative binomial distribution was used, suggesting this finding was not sensitive to the Poisson observation model.
source: Strong accumulation noise in the joint model was also found when the negative binomial distribution, a more flexible observation model, was used, suggesting that this finding was not sensitive to the Poisson observation model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a robustness check using an alternative observation model shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in diffusive noise between the joint and choice-only models suggest that accumulation dynamics underlying neural activity is impacted by noise that is resolved at the level of a behavioral accumulator model.
source: Differences in diffusive noise between the joint and choice-only models suggest that accumulation dynamics underlying neural activity is impacted by noise that is resolved at the level of a behavioral accumulator model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences in noise parameters between models.

claim: There was no significant difference in the value of λ across the cohorts of animals in the choice-only model.
source: Although there was no significant difference in the value of λ across the cohorts of animals in the choice-only model, we found substantial differences across brain regions in the joint model fits (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes a comparison of the leak parameter across animals for choice-only models shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Substantial differences in λ were found across brain regions in the joint model fits.
source: Although there was no significant difference in the value of λ across the cohorts of animals in the choice-only model, we found substantial differences across brain regions in the joint model fits (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes differences in the leak parameter across brain regions for joint models shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The PPC and ADS data were best fit by leaky accumulator models (λ<0).
source: The PPC and ADS data were best fit by leaky accumulator models (λ<0).
evidence: This describes the sign of the leak parameter for PPC and ADS.

claim: The FOF data was best described by a model with unstable accumulation dynamics (λ>0).
source: Surprisingly however, the FOF data was best described by a model with unstable accumulation dynamics (λ>0) meaning that the model's accumulator (and thus firing rates) are more strongly affected by early stimulus clicks.
evidence: This describes the sign of the leak parameter for FOF and its interpretation.

claim: The stronger weighting of earlier clicks in FOF was compounded by the low accumulation bound of the model that best described FOF data.
source: The stronger weighting of earlier clicks was compounded further by the low accumulation bound of the model that best described FOF data.
evidence: This describes an additional parameter finding for FOF and its relationship to the leak parameter.

claim: A low bound in conjunction with unstable accumulation causes a(t) to stop evolving early in the trial.
source: Such a low bound, in conjunction with unstable accumulation, causes a(t) to stop evolving early in the trial (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the consequence of the parameter combination shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The combination of low bound and unstable accumulation results in 'primacy encoding', in which early clicks more strongly impact the animal's choice while later clicks are ignored.
source: This results in a phenomenon known as 'primacy encoding', in which early clicks more strongly impact the animal's choice while later clicks are ignored.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model dynamics for FOF.

claim: The primacy encoding finding in FOF was confirmed using a generalized linear model (GLM).
source: We confirmed this finding in the FOF using a generalized linear model (GLM; see Methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a validation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The primacy encoding result is consistent with previous work suggesting that the FOF has a categorical representation of a(t).
source: This result is consistent with previous work suggesting that the FOF has a categorical representation of a(t) (Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This relates the current finding to prior work with a citation.

claim: All three brain regions were best described by accumulator models that differed in their best fitting parameters and exhibited dramatically different accumulation dynamics.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that all three brain regions were best described by accumulator models that differed in their best fitting parameters (and thus exhibit dramatically different accumulation dynamics)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about differences across brain regions.

claim: Each brain region's data was best described by a model that differed from that which best described accumulation at the level of the animal's choice.
source: and that each region's data was likewise best described by a model that differed from that which best described accumulation at the level of the animal's choice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion comparing neural and behavioral models.

claim: The maximum likelihood parameters for the shared-noise and independent-noise models for both FOF and ADS were similar, except for the initial accumulator variance parameter which differed significantly.
source: The maximum likelihood parameters for the two models for both regions were similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), except for the initial accumulator variance parameter which differed significantly.
evidence: This describes a comparison of parameters between two model variants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The independent-noise model provided a better description of choices and neural activity from ADS.
source: Comparing the cross-validated log-likelihood, we found that the independent-noise model provided a better description of choices and neural activity from ADS
evidence: This describes a model comparison result using cross-validation.

claim: The shared-noise model provided a slightly better description of FOF data.
source: while the shared-noise model provided a slightly better description of FOF data (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes a model comparison result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neural responses within the ADS reflect independent accumulation processes.
source: This finding supports the conclusion that neural responses within the ADS reflect independent accumulation processes
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison favoring independent-noise for ADS.

claim: Neurons in the FOF reflect a single latent accumulator.
source: while neurons in the FOF reflect a single latent accumulator.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison favoring shared-noise for FOF.

claim: When the number of neurons in ADS datasets was subsampled to match the maximum number of neurons in FOF sessions (three neurons), the ADS recordings still favored an independent-noise accumulator model.
source: Although ADS datasets with four or more neurons provided the primary contribution to these results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), when the number of neurons in ADS datasets was subsampled to match the maximum number of neurons in FOF sessions (three neurons), the ADS recordings still favored an independent-noise accumulator model (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes a control analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The difference between shared-noise and independent-noise models for ADS is not due to contributions from the animal's choice.
source: We fit the shared-noise and independent-noise model to neural data only (excluding choice data) and found consistent results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), suggesting this difference is not due to contributions from the animal's choice, which was modeled differently in each model (see above).
evidence: This describes a control analysis excluding choice data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Both shared and independent-noise accumulator models provided approximately equally accurate fits to the shuffle-corrected cross-correlations.
source: Across all pairs of simultaneously recorded neurons (70 pairs in total), we found that the shared and independent-noise accumulator models provided approximately equally accurate fits to the shuffle-corrected cross-correlations (mean r of 0.55 for shared model and 0.57 for independent-noise model for FOF; 0.63 for shared model and 0.60 for independent-noise model for ADS).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model fits to cross-correlation functions.

claim: Both models capture correlations in trial-to-trial neural responses beyond those accounted for by the PSTH.
source: This shows that both models capture correlations in trial-to-trial neural responses beyond those accounted for by the PSTH.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-correlation analysis results.

claim: The correlations captured by both models are primarily stimulus-induced and not a manifestation of non-stimulus-induced noise correlations, which are weak if present at all.
source: Although FOF weakly favored a shared-noise model and ADS favored an independent-noise model (Figure 4B) the comparable ability for each model to capture the shuffle-corrected cross-correlation function for each region suggests that these correlations are primarily stimulus-induced and not a manifestation of non-stimulus-induced (i.e., 'noise') correlations, which are weak if present at all.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-correlation analysis in the context of model comparisons.

claim: Responses in ADS had higher dimensionality than in FOF.
source: Consistent with our modeling results, we found that responses in ADS had higher dimensionality than in FOF (i.e., ADS exhibited less firing rate covariation)
evidence: This describes a dimensionality analysis result using participation ratio.

claim: ADS sessions with greater dimensionality were those that favored the independent-noise model.
source: and that ADS sessions with greater dimensionality were those that favored the independent-noise model (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This describes a relationship between dimensionality and model preference shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The choice data posterior was broad, meaning a large set of a(t) trajectories were all consistent with the animal's choice.
source: The choice data posterior was broad; a large set of a(t) trajectories were all consistent with the animal's choice.
evidence: This describes the posterior distribution when only choice data is used.

claim: When both choice and neural spiking activity were considered, a substantially narrower distribution over a(t) was obtained.
source: However, when we considered both choice and neural spiking activity, we obtained a substantially narrower distribution over a(t), meaning including neural data in the joint model offers greater confidence in the precise value of accumulated evidence at each moment within a trial.
evidence: This describes the posterior distribution when both choice and neural data are used.

claim: For all brain regions, the median posterior standard deviation given neural data and choice was substantially smaller than when conditioning only on choice (median difference FOF: 0.46; PPC: 0.72; ADS: 2.23).
source: For all brain regions, the median posterior standard deviation given neural data and choice was substantially smaller than when conditioning only on choice (Figure 5B; median difference FOF: 0.46; PPC: 0.72; ADS: 2.23).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of posterior uncertainty shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reduction in the posterior width increased with the number of neurons.
source: This reduction in the posterior width increased with the number of neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes a relationship between number of neurons and posterior uncertainty shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Choices could be predicted more accurately under the joint model than under the choice model for all three brain regions.
source: We found that choices could be predicted more accurately under the joint model, which took into account the stimulus, neural activity, and choices, than under the choice model, which used stimulus information and choices alone.
evidence: This describes a comparison of choice prediction accuracy between models.

claim: The joint model of FOF data showed an almost 50% improvement in test log-likelihood and a 6% increase in prediction accuracy compared to the choice model.
source: The joint model had higher test log-likelihood for choice data and choice-prediction accuracy for all three brain regions, with the joint model of FOF data showing an almost 50% improvement in test log-likelihood and a 6% increase in prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance for FOF.

claim: Decoding under the joint accumulator model significantly outperformed logistic regression.
source: We compared our accumulator-based joint model to a logistic regression model (i.e., Bernoulli GLM) which used the final accumulated click difference and the trial-summed spike count for each neuron as regressors (Methods). Decoding under the joint accumulator model significantly outperformed logistic regression (Figure 6A, GLM).
evidence: This describes a comparison to a baseline GLM model shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The performance of the GLM did not depend strongly on the time window considered.
source: The performance of the GLM did not depend strongly on the time window considered: decoding of choice using spikes from the last 50 ms (Figure 6A, GLM 50 ms), 100 ms, 150 ms, 200 ms, and 250 ms before a decision all performed similarly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a control analysis varying time windows shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The joint accumulation framework and fine timescale dynamics captures features of spike trains useful for predicting the animal's choice, above and beyond the information carried by spike counts in particular time windows before the choice.
source: This shows that the joint accumulation framework and the fine timescale dynamics of the joint model captures features of the spike trains that are useful for predicting the animal's choice, above and beyond the information carried by spike counts in particular time windows before the choice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison to GLM models.

claim: Sign changes in the cumulative click difference were rare.
source: Sign changes in the cumulative click difference were rare, as were putative change of mind events under the choice-only model, both of which could only be caused by the stimulus (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes the frequency of sign changes in the stimulus shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Putative change of mind events were rare under the choice-only model.
source: Sign changes in the cumulative click difference were rare, as were putative change of mind events under the choice-only model, both of which could only be caused by the stimulus (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes the frequency of putative change of mind events for the choice-only model shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Putative change of mind events were observed frequently under the joint model for all three brain regions.
source: In contrast, putative change of mind events were observed frequently under the joint model for all three brain regions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes the frequency of putative change of mind events for the joint model shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Putative change of mind events reflect information about the accumulator carried in neural activity.
source: This shows that putative change of mind events reflect information about the accumulator carried in neural activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the difference in change of mind frequency between models.

claim: Putative change of mind events were observed least frequently in the FOF and most frequently in the ADS.
source: Putative change of mind events were observed least frequently in the FOF and most frequently in the ADS (Figure 6D)
evidence: This describes a comparison of change of mind frequency across brain regions shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The animal's performance improved on putative change of mind event trials (fraction correct: FOF: 0.88 vs 0.74; PPC: 0.87 vs 0.74; ADS: 0.85 vs 0.76).
source: The animal's performance improved on putative change of mind event trials (fraction correct: FOF: 0.88 vs 0.74; PPC: 0.87 vs 0.74; ADS: 0.85 vs 0.76; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of animal accuracy shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The choice prediction of the joint model was more accurate on putative change of mind event trials (fraction correct: FOF: 0.92 vs 0.80; PPC: 0.88 vs 0.77; ADS: 0.88 vs 0.78).
source: and the choice prediction of the joint model was also more accurate (fraction correct: FOF: 0.92 vs 0.80; PPC: 0.88 vs 0.77; ADS: 0.88 vs 0.78; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model accuracy shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The decision-making dynamics that give rise to putative change of mind events primarily correct incorrect decision-making dynamics early within a trial.
source: suggesting that the decision-making dynamics that give rise to these events primarily correct incorrect decision-making dynamics early within a trial.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the improved accuracy on change of mind trials.

claim: Initial variability in the accumulation dynamics was greater in both PPC and ADS, regions for which putative changes of mind were more likely.
source: Initial variability in the accumulation dynamics, as reflected in neural responses, was found to be greater in both PPC and ADS (Figure 3A), regions for which putative changes of mind were more likely (Figure 6D), consistent with this assumption.
evidence: This relates initial variance parameters to change of mind frequency across regions.

claim: Putative change of mind events were more likely to occur at later moments in the trial, usually not long before the stimulus ended.
source: Furthermore, putative change of mind events were more likely to occur at later moments in the trial, usually not long before the stimulus ended (Figure 6E)
evidence: This describes the temporal distribution of change of mind events shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A statistically significant effect was found for PPC (p<0.003) and ADS (p<0.0008) showing slower response time when a change of mind event occurred closer to the end of the stimulus.
source: We found a statistically significant effect for the PPC and the ADS (PPC: p<0.003; ADS: p<0.0008; two-sided t-test), which both showed a slower response time when a change of mind event occurred closer to the end of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a statistical test result relating change of mind timing to response latency.

claim: The dynamics of accumulation that best-fit choices and neural data from each brain region differed significantly across brain regions.
source: We fit the model to data from three brain regions and found that the dynamics of accumulation that best-fit choices and neural data from each brain region differed significantly across brain regions
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the model fitting results.

claim: The accumulation dynamics that best-fit each brain region all differed from the accumulation model that best described the animal's choices.
source: and from the accumulation model that best described the animal's choices.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion comparing neural and behavioral models.

claim: Prior analysis of these data found that the ADS represented accumulated evidence in a graded manner.
source: Prior analysis of these data found that the anterodorsal striatum (ADS) represented accumulated evidence in a graded manner (Yartsev et al., 2018)
evidence: This cites a prior finding about ADS from earlier analysis of the same data.

claim: Prior analysis found that the FOF represented choice more categorically.
source: while the frontal orienting fields (FOF) represented choice more categorically (Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites a prior finding about FOF from earlier analysis of the same data.

claim: The current analysis confirms the ADS as a veracious representation of accumulated evidence.
source: Our analysis confirms the ADS as a veracious representation of accumulated evidence
evidence: This is a conclusion about ADS based on the current analysis.

claim: The accumulation model that best described FOF activity was dynamically unstable, producing neural responses that looked like a categorical representation of choice but that were in fact unstable accumulators sensitive to early stimulus information.
source: while offering a more nuanced view of the FOF: the accumulation model that best described FOF activity was dynamically unstable, producing neural responses that looked like a categorical representation of choice but that were in fact unstable accumulators sensitive to early stimulus information.
evidence: This is a conclusion about FOF based on the current analysis.

claim: Neural correlates of graded evidence accumulation were identified in PPC, albeit more weakly than in the ADS.
source: Additionally, we analyzed recordings from the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), a brain region long studied in connection to evidence accumulation (Hanks et al., 2015; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001), where we identified neural correlates of graded evidence accumulation, albeit more weakly than in the ADS.
evidence: This is a conclusion about PPC based on the current analysis with citations to prior work on PPC.

claim: Incorporating neural activity into accumulation models reduced the uncertainty in the moment-by-moment value of accumulated evidence when compared to models fit only to animal choices.
source: Incorporating neural activity into accumulation models reduced the uncertainty in the moment-by-moment value of accumulated evidence when compared to models fit only to animal choices.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the benefit of including neural data.

claim: The reduction in uncertainty led to a more refined picture of the moment-by-moment value of accumulated evidence, which made the model more informative about what choice the animal intended to make.
source: This reduction in uncertainty led to a more refined picture of the moment-by-moment value of accumulated evidence, which made the model more informative about what choice the animal intended to make.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the consequence of reduced uncertainty.

claim: The novel analysis revealed extensive choice vacillation reflected in ADS activity.
source: Our model allowed us to implement a novel analysis to examine how subject provisional choice changed during individual trials, commonly referred to as 'changes of mind' (Boyd-Meredith et al., 2022; Kiani et al., 2014; Peixoto et al., 2021), that revealed extensive choice vacillation reflected in ADS activity
evidence: This describes a finding from the change of mind analysis with citations to related work.

claim: The novel analysis revealed greater choice certainty reflected in FOF activity.
source: and greater choice certainty reflected in FOF activity.
evidence: This describes a finding from the change of mind analysis.

claim: Different brain regions represent accumulated evidence in dramatically different ways.
source: Our results suggest that different brain regions represent accumulated evidence in dramatically different ways
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Accumulation at the whole-animal level may be constructed from a variety of neural-level accumulators.
source: and that accumulation at the whole-animal level may be constructed from a variety of neural-level accumulators.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Previous studies relating neural data to behaviorally inferred accumulation dynamics have implicitly assumed that individual brain regions reflect the whole-animal level accumulator.
source: Previous studies relating neural data to behaviorally inferred accumulation dynamics have implicitly assumed that individual brain regions reflect the whole-animal level accumulator.
evidence: This is a critique of assumptions in prior work.

claim: Choice data from evidence accumulation tasks have allowed for the development of sophisticated models of animals' accumulation strategies.
source: Choice data from evidence accumulation tasks e.g., Brunton et al., 2013; Raposo et al., 2012; Sanders and Kepecs, 2012 have allowed for the development of sophisticated models of animals' accumulation strategies (e.g., Bogacz et al., 2006; Brunton et al., 2013; Genkin et al., 2021; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff et al., 2016; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Shinn et al., 2020; Wiecki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work with multiple citations.

claim: Neural correlates of accumulated evidence have been found in a wide variety of brain regions.
source: In parallel, neural correlates of accumulated evidence have been found in a wide variety of brain regions (e.g., Brody and Hanks, 2016; Churchland et al., 2011; Ding and Gold, 2010; Erlich et al., 2011; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Hanks et al., 2015; Huk and Shadlen, 2005; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Mante et al., 2013; Ratcliff et al., 2003; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Yartsev et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a statement about prior work with multiple citations.

claim: Methods have been developed to describe the statistical relationship between neural activity and accumulated evidence.
source: and methods have been developed to describe the statistical relationship between neural activity and accumulated evidence (e.g., Aoi et al., 2020; Beck et al., 2008; Churchland et al., 2011; Hanks et al., 2015; Latimer et al., 2015; Latimer and Freedman, 2021; Park et al., 2014; Zoltowski et al., 2019; Zoltowski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work with multiple citations.

claim: Few analysis methods which use precise spike timing information take into account the timing of stimulus information or use choice data directly.
source: For example, few analysis methods which use precise spike timing information take into account the timing of stimulus information or use choice data directly (e.g., Latimer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a critique of prior methods with a citation.

claim: Few methods that use the precise timing of stimulus information to infer accumulated evidence use neural responses directly.
source: Likewise few methods that use the precise timing of stimulus information to infer accumulated evidence use neural responses directly (e.g., Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a critique of prior methods with a citation.

claim: The evidence accumulation process inferred from behavioral data alone need not correspond to the accumulation process that best matches data from a single brain region.
source: The evidence accumulation process inferred from behavioral data alone need not correspond to the accumulation process that best matches data from a single brain region; behavior is the result of interactions between multiple brain regions.
evidence: This is a conceptual argument about the relationship between behavioral and neural accumulation.

claim: Two brain regions, one favoring accumulation of early evidence and the other favoring accumulation of late evidence, could together support stable behavior-level accumulation.
source: For example, two brain regions, one favoring accumulation of early evidence (e.g., an unstable accumulator) and the other favoring accumulation of late evidence (e.g., a leaky accumulator) could together support stable behavior-level accumulation.
evidence: This is a hypothetical example illustrating how different regional dynamics could combine.

claim: A primacy encoding model of the FOF is supported by the change of mind analysis.
source: A primacy encoding model of the FOF is supported by our change of mind analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion relating the change of mind analysis to the FOF model.

claim: Putative change of mind events identified from neural activity occurred less frequently in the FOF than other regions (p<4.5694e-82 FOF vs. PPC; p<3.4585e-323 FOF vs. ADS; Fisher's exact test).
source: Putative change of mind events identified from neural activity occurred less frequently in the FOF than other regions (p<4.5694e-82 FOF vs. PPC; p<3.4585e-323 FOF vs. ADS; Fisher's exact test) consistent with an early-commitment strategy in the FOF.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of change of mind frequency across regions.

claim: A recent study found that FOF activity reflected evidence across stimulus-induced 'overt' changes of mind, and that these events were common in the FOF.
source: A recent study of the FOF during an accumulation task in which evidence dynamically changed throughout a trial found that FOF activity reflected evidence across stimulus-induced 'overt' changes of mind, and that these events were common in the FOF (Boyd-Meredith et al., 2022).
evidence: This cites a finding from a recent related study.

claim: FOF reflects evidence across changes of mind, but non-stimulus-induced 'covert' changes of mind were rarely occurring during a task in which the evidence was static.

claim: The framework can be extended to describe additional physiological or behavioral variables.
source: Although we have extended the evidence accumulation model to include neural responses and choice, we could extend it further to describe additional physiological or behavioral variables (e.g., from annotated video data, pupil-dilation measurements, response time, etc.).

claim: The framework can readily accept modifications and extensions of its dynamical equations.
source: Although we considered a specific evidence accumulation model due to its normative interpretation, our framework can readily accept modifications and extensions of its dynamical equations (e.g., Genkin et al., 2021).

source: Our framework can also accommodate more elaborate and/or appropriate relationships between accumulated evidence and neural responses, as we briefly explored by considering the negative binomial distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The framework can be adapted to any task where noisy temporal accumulation of evidence is thought to play a role.
source: Although our framework was developed with the specific application to a pulse-based accumulation task in mind, it is not confined to this. Our framework can be adapted to any task where noisy temporal accumulation of evidence is thought to play a role, and for which neural recordings and behavioral choices reflect this process (Aguillon-Rodriguez et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the generalizability of the framework with citation.
